analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue vaccine makers for injuries from government-mandated vaccines.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2022 with a single cosponsor and never received a committee vote or floor action before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would remove the legal shield that protects vaccine manufacturers from lawsuits when a government body, government official, or any organization receiving government money requires a vaccine. Anyone injured or killed by such a vaccine could sue the manufacturer directly in state or federal court, without first filing a claim through the federal Vaccine Injury Compensation Program. It would also bar the Health and Human Services Secretary from adding a vaccine to the program's injury table if that vaccine is required by the government and given without informed consent or without a religious or medical exemption.
analysis.who_benefits: People who suffer injuries or deaths from a vaccine that was required by a government agency, a government official, or any entity receiving federal or state funding. Under current law, they generally cannot sue the manufacturer and are limited to the federal Vaccine Injury Compensation Program; this bill would let them take manufacturers and distributors to court instead.

how_it_helps.text: Strips the liability shield (the no-suit protection for pandemic and epidemic products) from any licensed or emergency-authorized vaccine that a federal or state government, an official, or a federally or state-funded entity requires, or penalizes refusal of [S3].

Allows individuals to sue vaccine manufacturers and distributors in state or federal court directly, without first seeking compensation through the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program, for injuries or deaths from such mandated vaccines [S2].

Bars the Secretary of Health and Human Services from adding a vaccine to the Vaccine Injury Table if the vaccine is required by the federal government or a federally funded entity and was administered without informed consent or without a requested religious or medical exemption [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Vaccine manufacturers and distributors, who would lose the liability protection they currently hold for any vaccine that a government or government-funded entity mandates, and could face jury awards in civil court. Vaccine programs that depend on steady, affordable supply could face higher prices or reduced availability, a cost that would ultimately reach public health budgets and consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Vaccine manufacturers and public vaccine programs

drawbacks.text: The bill removes liability protection only for vaccines someone is compelled to take, while leaving it in place for vaccines people choose; manufacturers could respond to the added court exposure by raising vaccine prices or withdrawing products, since the existing shield was designed to keep vaccine supply steady and affordable [S3].

Bypassing the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program moves injury claims into ordinary courts, which are typically slower and more expensive for injured people, and the bill's exemption and consent conditions apply only to vaccines added to the program's table, not the existing ones [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives a real right of redress to a narrow group: people injured by a vaccine their government or a government-funded institution required them to take, who today are channeled into the federal compensation program and cannot sue. That right comes at the cost of exposing manufacturers to open-ended court liability for exactly those vaccines, which could raise vaccine prices or shrink supply. The bill was written to cover a narrow set of circumstances, but its effects on the vaccine market would not be narrow, and it received no serious consideration or refinement in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: the House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and no vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Louie Gohmert introduced the bill in the House on November 30, 2022 [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on December 1, 2022, to the Subcommittee on Health [S5].
It drew one cosponsor, a House Republican [S4].
No further action was taken, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the bill receiving a committee vote or floor action [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Vaccine manufacturers, who keep the liability protection the bill would have removed for mandated vaccines, and who face no court exposure from it.

for.name: Rep. Louie Gohmert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only named sponsor.

for.name: 1 House Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it drew.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Frank Pallone (D-NJ)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and took no further action — no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republicans were on record supporting the bill and no one is recorded opposing it; it never advanced far enough for any vote that would show a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would strip their immunity from suit for any licensed or emergency-authorized vaccine that a government or government-funded entity mandates, letting injured people sue in court instead of using the federal compensation program. The industry's interest in keeping that shield runs against the interest of people who want their day in court over a mandated vaccine.

industries.industry: Government-funded institutions requiring vaccines (hospitals, schools, employers)
industries.note: Any entity receiving federal or state funding that requires a vaccine would trigger the bill's liability provision for the manufacturer, making mandates more legally fraught for such institutions. They face no liability themselves under the bill, but the rules governing their vaccine requirements would change.
